title: Using and Evaluating Textual Evidence
keyIdea: Back up every point about a text with exact words from it. Strong evidence is about the thing you are claiming and fits only one reading. Keep quotations short, build them into your own sentence, then explain which words prove your point and how.

kid: When you make a point about a text, you need proof. The proof is evidence: the exact words the writer used. Quote them, and the reader can check your idea for themselves.

Not all evidence is equal. Say your claim is that Maya is nervous. The hall was packed is weak, because it is about the room, not Maya. She gripped her script so hard that the pages crumpled is strong. It shows Maya herself, and it can only mean tension.

Keep quotations short. Pick only the words that do the work, then fit them into your own sentence: Maya gripped her script so hard that the pages crumpled. Do not just drop a whole line in after a full stop.
Then explain. Do not retell the quote, and do not just repeat your claim. Zoom in on a word. The verb gripped suggests force she cannot control, so her body gives her nerves away.
adult: This topic asks learners to back up points with exact words from a text. That covers what the text says and what we can work out from it. They also judge which quote best supports a point, and they explain the link. For ages 11 to 14, the goal moves from giving any quote to giving the one that fits best.

The lab splits the skill into parts. Learners match each claim to the line that proves it. They rate quotes as strong, weak or off the point. They cut a sentence down to the shortest quote that still works. They fit quotes into their own sentences. Last, they pick the explanation that looks closely at a word.

Common mistakes: picking a quote about the setting or a different person, not the one in the claim; picking a quote that is true but beside the point; thinking a long quote is a strong one; dropping a quote in as its own sentence; retelling the quote or repeating the claim instead of explaining it; and treating a guess as if the text said it.
Ask your learner why one quote is better than another. Good answers say whether it is about the right person, whether it could mean something else, and which single word carries the meaning.

familyTip: When your child says something about a book, film or song, ask "Which exact words make you think that?" and then "Is there a line that proves it even better?"

practice.prompt: Claim: Priya is exhausted. Which evidence is strongest?
choices: “Her eyelids drooped as she slumped over the desk.”
“The classroom clock ticked loudly.”
“Priya had a blue pencil case.”
practice.hint: Which quotation is about Priya herself and can only mean tiredness?
practice.explain: Drooping eyelids and slumping show tiredness in Priya herself. The clock is setting, and the pencil case is irrelevant.

practice.prompt: Ravi “checked his phone {n} times” during the film. Is this good evidence that he is bored?
choices: Yes: a repeated action that shows it
No: it only mentions a phone
No: numbers can not be evidence
practice.hint: Does the action happen once or again and again, and what does that suggest?
practice.explain: Checking a phone {n} times is a repeated action by Ravi, so it is strong evidence of boredom or distraction.

practice.prompt: Which sentence embeds the quotation correctly?
choices: The sea “roared against the rocks”, which makes it sound dangerous.
The sea is dangerous. “The sea roared against the rocks all night.”
The sea is dangerous “roared”.
practice.hint: Read each one aloud. Which still sounds like one proper sentence?
practice.explain: The first one fits the quotation into its own grammar. The second drops a whole line in, and the third breaks the sentence.

practice.prompt: Your quotation is {n} words long, but only 4 of them prove your point. What should you do?
choices: Cut it down to the words that prove it
Keep all {n} words
Add more words around it
practice.hint: Is a longer quotation stronger, or just harder to analyse?
practice.explain: Cut the {n} words down to the ones that do the work. Length does not make evidence stronger.

pool.prompt: Claim: Sam is excited about the trip. Which evidence is strongest?
choices: “Sam bounced on her toes, grinning at the coach.”
“The coach was late.”
“Sam wore a green coat.”
pool.hint: Which quotation shows Sam herself, and fits excitement?
pool.explain: Bouncing and grinning show Sam herself and suggest excitement. The late coach is setting, and the coat is irrelevant.

pool.prompt: Which explanation analyses the quotation “he crept down the stairs”?
choices: “Crept” suggests he does not want to be heard.
This shows that he crept down the stairs.
This shows that he is sneaky.
pool.hint: One retells, one repeats a claim, one zooms in on a word. Which zooms in?
pool.explain: Analysis names the word and what it suggests. The others retell the quotation or repeat the claim.

pool.prompt: The text says “Kai’s hands were shaking.” Is “Kai is afraid” stated or inferred?
choices: Inferred: the shaking is a clue
Stated: the text says so
Neither: we can not use it
pool.hint: Does the text actually use the word afraid?
pool.explain: The text states the shaking hands. Fear is an inference from that clue, and it is a fair one.

pool.prompt: Why is “Zara read every book in the library twice” strong evidence that she loves reading?
choices: It shows a habit kept up over time
Because it is a long quotation
Because it mentions books
pool.hint: What does every book, twice, tell you about how often?
pool.explain: It shows a repeated choice over a long time, which is what loving reading looks like. Length and topic words do not make it strong.

pool.prompt: Ellie “gave away {n} of her own books”. Which sentence embeds this correctly?
choices: Ellie “gave away {n} of her own books”, which shows her generosity.
Ellie is generous. “She gave away {n} of her own books.”
Ellie is generous “books”.
pool.hint: Which one reads as a single smooth sentence?
pool.explain: The first fits the quotation into its own sentence. The second is dropped in, and the third breaks the grammar.

pool.prompt: Claim: Dev is hungry. Which quotation is best trimmed?
choices: “his stomach growled”
the whole page about the kitchen
pool.hint: Which one keeps the proof and drops the rest?
pool.explain: His stomach growled is short and proves the point. A whole page is too long, and a proves nothing.

pool.prompt: Mr Hale “sighed {n} times” in the meeting. Which explanation analyses this?
choices: Repeated sighing suggests his patience is running out.
This shows he sighed {n} times.
This shows he is impatient.
pool.hint: Which one says what the action suggests, not just what happened?
pool.explain: Saying that repeated sighing suggests patience running out is analysis. The others retell or restate.

pool.prompt: Claim: Nia is brave. Which evidence does NOT support it?
choices: “Nia had red hair.”
“Nia stepped forward when no one else would.”
“Her voice shook, but she kept speaking.”
pool.hint: Which line has nothing to do with bravery?
pool.explain: Red hair is true but irrelevant. Stepping forward and speaking through fear both show courage.

visual.caption: Claim: Ben is jealous of his brother. How well does each quotation support it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: “Ben glared at his brother’s new bike.”

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the line that proves a claim, rate quotations, trim a quotation, embed it in your own sentence and explain it.
